extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and educated readers interested in epic poetry and poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and critical guidance for composing and evaluating epic/heroic poems (fable, characters, sentiments, and language), grounded in Aristotelian poetics and exemplified by Homer, Virgil, Milton, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable: suitability of the event (happy vs unhappy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first imperfection observed is that the Event of the poem is unhappy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether an epic's fable is appropriate: Aristotle's taxonomy (simple vs implex) shows that many perfect implex fables end unhappily (good→bad), which is apt for tragedy but may be less proper for heroic/epic poems. Milton's Paradise Lost has an unhappy event (the Fall), which some see as an imperfection in an epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fable type: simple vs implex (change of fortune)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Fable of every Poem is either Simple (no change of fortune) or Implex (the chief actor's fortune changes from Bad to Good or Good to Bad).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implex fables (change of fortune) are thought most perfect because they stir passions and surprise the reader. Implex divides into two kinds: (1) rise (misfortune to prosperity, e.g., Ulysses) and (2) fall (honour to misery, e.g., Oedipus/Adam and Eve). Choose the kind that best serves the emotional and formal aims of the poem (tragic falls suit tragedy; heroic epics often prefer other treatments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate identification of the Hero
rubrics_metrics.description: The poem's hero must match the kind of action the poet intends; searching for a conventional heroic figure where none was intended is a mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's Paradise Lost is an epic/narrative in which the Messiah, rather than Adam or Satan, can be seen as the proper hero. Critics who expect a conventional heroic protagonist (like Achilles) misunderstand Milton's design. Make clear who functions as the central heroic agent in the poem's principal action and episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and plausibility of allegorical particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain particulars in the texture of the fable lack probability for an epic (e.g., the actions ascribed to Sin and Death, the picture of the Limbo of Vanity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid allegories or incidents that strain plausibility within the epic's register; such passages may read as Spenserian or Ariostan rather than Homeric/Virgilian. Allegorical figures must be integrated believably into the poem's world or clearly framed as fable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive digressions from the main fable
rubrics_metrics.description: In the structure of his Poem he has likewise admitted of too many Digressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic poets should minimize digressions that interrupt narrative momentum. Aristotle advises that the poet should seldom speak himself and should put as much as possible into the mouths of principal actors. Exceptions are allowable when a digression directly clarifies or reinforces a central incident (Virgil's Turnus/ Pallas reflection is justified because it deepens the main event); by contrast, Lucan's frequent diverticula are injudicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize authorial reflection and self-address
rubrics_metrics.description: The Poet should, as much as possible, speak little himself and not let his narration sleep for the sake of reflections of his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial intrusions that pause the story are generally faults unless they serve a clear purpose in highlighting or preserving a crucial incident for the reader. Let characters and events carry the narrative voice when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and regularity of design; greatness of plan
rubrics_metrics.description: An epic should possess greatness of plan, regularity of design, and masterly beauties similar to Homer and Virgil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the poem's overall plan is grand and coherent. Regularity of design connects episodes and digressions to the main action, producing the 'greatness of plan' expected in exemplary epic poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overly pointed sentiments and puns
rubrics_metrics.description: Some sentiments are too much pointed, and some degenerate even into puns (e.g., the pigmies line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain dignity and gravity appropriate to epic subject-matter; avoid cheap verbal jokes, pointed witticisms, or puns that reduce seriousness or the reader's sense of sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unframed pagan/allusive matter presented as literal truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent allusion to Heathen Fables which are not of a piece with the Divine Subject; such allusions are acceptable when represented as fabulous but not when presented as truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using pagan myths or classical fables in a religious/divine epic, clearly mark their status (mythical/fabulous) rather than mingling them as literal cosmological facts. Unqualified heathen allusions can undermine the poem's thematic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of learning; avoid ostentatious display of scholarship
rubrics_metrics.description: An unnecessary ostentation of learning occurs frequently; Homer and Virgil conceal learning, while Milton often displays it directly (Free-Will, Predestination, history, astronomy, geography).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let erudition appear naturally in the poem rather than as explicit didactic excursions. Learned digressions should be woven subtly into character-speech or action; avoid lengthy displays that read as the poet showing off scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity: avoid language that is too laboured, archaic, or obscured
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's language is often too much laboured, and sometimes obscured by old words, transpositions, and foreign idioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for diction that conveys sublime ideas intelligibly. Overuse of archaic words, inverted syntax, or foreign idioms may obscure meaning. While elevated diction is appropriate, clarity for ordinary readers should be a goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid verbal jingles and trivial repetitions
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet often affects a kind of Jingle in his Words (e.g., 'a World of Woe', 'begirt th' Almighty throne / Beseeching or besieging').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Figures that create pleasing sound (paronomasia, internal echo) can become poor and trifling if overused; modern polite writing tends to reject such 'jingle' when it undermines seriousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive technical terms and terms of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent use of Technical Words or Terms of Art (Doric Pillars, Pilasters; Eccentric, trepidation, ecliptic) is noted as a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should make abstruse or technical matters intelligible to ordinary readers. Avoid piling on specialized vocabulary from architecture, astronomy, or other arts unless those terms are necessary and made clear by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make hard and abstruse subjects intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is one of the great Beauties of Poetry to make hard things intelligible, and to deliver what is abstruse in such easy Language as may be understood by ordinary Readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for expressive clarity: complex theological, philosophical, or technical content should be conveyed through evocative, accessible language rather than obscure jargon or merely learned display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of digressions only to support the main action (justifiable exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some reflections that suspend narration may be allowable when they prevent a small incident from being forgotten and so serve the great event (Virgil's reflection on Turnus dressing in Pallas's spoils).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When digressing, ensure the material directly reinforces the principal action or preserves a crucial causal link. Such well-placed reflections strengthen the reader's grasp of central occurrences; gratuitous digressions (ascribed to Lucan) are injudicious.
